cert-machine · report · every number recomputed at build

The glide ring is unfalsifiable. That is the problem with it.

When the engine quits, the panel draws one ring and calls it your reach — one glide ratio, one forecast wind, one weight, rendered as a promise. Recomputed as an enclosure over those same inputs’ uncertainty, on a real pinned flight: 57% of the airfields inside that line cannot be proved reachable. None of them can be proved unreachable either, and that is not a coincidence — while the line’s assumptions sit inside the envelope, it is incapable of being wrong.

tl;dr
  • The finding. 57% of the sites inside the single-line ring are not proved reachable — and zero are proved unreachable. Across 36 cruise states of a pinned PC12 flight at the 35 kt preset, the line shows 3974 site-states as within reach; the certified band proves 1694 and leaves 2280 undecided. The zero is structural and the build asserts it: while the line’s inputs lie inside the envelope, nothing inside it can be refuted, so the line can never be caught being wrong. Reverse the winds-aloft forecast — a documented failure of the one input it leans on hardest — and 1356 site-states inside that same line become provably out of reach.
  • The mechanism. Outward-rounded interval arithmetic over the glide model, with the box subdivided 24×12 so the answer is not charged for a dependency the physics does not have. Both outer verdicts are conservative: a wider enclosure can only move a site INTO undecided, never into a wrong answer.
  • Check it. node apps/glide-band/battery.js — 18 checks including a 4000-draw containment test, and 4 red controls that must fire, among them the point-estimate method itself.

§1 · the instrument

One flight, 650 airfields, three verdicts

Scrub the slider to fly the cruise. The dashed line is what a panel draws from point estimates. The filled boundary is the certified inner ring — every airfield inside it is reachable for every value in the stated envelope. The outer boundary is refutation: beyond it, no value in the envelope reaches. The hatched annulus between them is the part nobody currently shows you, and it is where the dashed line spends most of its length.

§2 · the comparison

What the single line hides

The comparison is not "their number versus our number" — both come from the same physics and the same flight. It is a comparison of methods: one input value each, versus the range each input actually has. Nothing here asserts what any particular product computes internally; what is compared is the point-estimate method, which is what every shipped glide ring draws.

The first half of the comparison is the uncomfortable one, and it is about logic rather than arithmetic. While the panel’s assumed glide ratio, airspeed and wind sit anywhere inside the honest envelope, its line always falls between the two certified boundaries — the build asserts this and refuses if it ever fails. So no airfield inside that line can be proved unreachable. The line is never caught being wrong, and it is never shown to be right either: 57% of what it claims is simply undecided by the evidence it was drawn from. An instrument that cannot fail a test is not passing one.

The second half is what happens when one input is not merely uncertain but wrong. Winds aloft is a forecast, and forecasts are sometimes reversed. Leave the panel drawing its ring from the forecast and let the envelope carry the wind that is actually there, 180° the other way: the line now reaches far past the outer boundary on what it believes is the downwind side. 1356 of the 3974 site-states it shows as reachable, 34%, are provably unreachable for every value in the envelope. Toggle “forecast 180° out” above and watch the crosses appear. Note what changed: the line did not become less accurate, it became FALSIFIABLE — and was falsified. That is the whole difference between the two instruments.

The sharpest single row in the sweep. At 23,975 ft with the 60 kt preset, KNEL — Lakehurst Maxfield Field Airport — lies 139.2 km away. The single line puts your reach at 140 km, so it draws that field comfortably inside. The certified band is 10–56 km: the field is beyond the outer boundary, so it is unreachable for every value in the envelope. Not uncertain — refuted.

Aggregated over the 36 cruise states at the 35 kt preset with the panel’s assumptions inside the envelope: the line shows 3974 site-states inside your reach, the band proves 1694 and leaves 2280 undecided. Under the reversed-forecast scenario the same sweep turns 1356 of them from undecided into refuted.

The undecided annulus is the product, not a defect. A wider band is not a worse answer; it is the same answer with its width shown. And every undecided row carries the disclosure that would settle it — the last column of the table is the glide ratio you would have to know you have. That turns a verdict into a request, which is the only part of this a pilot can act on in the air.

§3 · what is and is not claimed

Four hypotheses, stated rather than buried

H1 · terrain is not modelled. The band is glide distance over ground at the field’s own elevation. Rising ground between here and there can only REMOVE reach, so the asymmetry is load-bearing and runs the safe way: REFUTED is unaffected by H1 and stays proved; PROVED REACHABLE carries H1 and means "reachable if the path is unobstructed". A terrain layer would move green fields to undecided and never the reverse.

H2 · steady state. Steady wind through the descent, steady-state glide, no pushover transient, no shear or thermal structure.

H3 · geometry. Great circles on a sphere whose radius is enclosed by [6356.752, 6378.137] km, pole to equator. Deliberately crude, deliberately conservative, and six orders of magnitude above the double-precision error of the haversine — so the geodesy needs no separate error argument.

H4 · the envelope is a stated scenario, not manufacturer data. No published performance figure for any aircraft is asserted anywhere here. The nominal glide ratio is 12.0 against an envelope of [10.2, 12.6] for propeller state, weight and speed-hold error; best-glide airspeed 100 kt against [92, 108]; altitude ±250 ft; forecast wind ±25% on speed and ±15° on direction. Move any of them and every number on this page moves with it. The finding is about the method, and it survives any envelope wider than a point.

wording

“Certified” on this page always means a mathematically certified enclosure — an interval proved to contain the true value. It carries no airworthiness meaning, no design assurance and no approval of any kind. The artifact says NOT FOR NAVIGATION on its face, and it means it: this is a demonstration of a decision procedure, on a flight that had no emergency.

§4 · the honest gap

What would have to be true for this to be in a cockpit

Three things this does not have, named so nobody has to ask. Terrain. H1 is the big one; a certified band with a terrain floor is the same arithmetic over a pinned DEM, and it is the next build rather than a research problem. Real performance data. The envelope here is stated, not measured; a manufacturer’s flight-test data would replace H4 with something narrower and the annulus would shrink accordingly — which is exactly the point, because the width is a measure of what is not known. Design assurance. Nothing here is DO-178C evidence, and the distance between an exact enclosure and certifiable software is the real cost in avionics.

What it does have is the part that is hard to buy: a verdict that cannot be argued with, an annulus that is honest about what is not known, and a published threshold that says what would settle it. The same arithmetic is what an exactly certified overbound for ARAIM protection levels would need — a proof that a nominal error distribution bounds the real one, in rational arithmetic rather than with margins and floating point. That is where the expensive line item is.
